This Transit Camper Van Has a Handcrafted Interior With Home-Like Comforts Hidden in Plain Sight
14 photos
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / LiamTheTerrible
There are endless ways in which you can customize a camper van. Some people prefer all-out luxurious builds that try to come as close to a conventional home, while others, like me, look for relatively simpler builds. The conversion I'd like to share with you today is part of the latter category.
What we have here is a build based on a 2022 Ford Transit with a high roof. It was created by Coalition Vans, a Sheffield, UK-based company specializing in custom camper van conversions. We've covered some of its projects here on autoevolution, such as a bespoke Transit-based mobile home .
On the outside, this Transit has few upgrades. The most significant ones are four tinted, double-glazed windows: two at the rear and two on the sides. By the way, since the vehicle is a right-hand-drive, the driver's side is the one on the right.
Other notable mods are an electric hookup point and rails on the roof that hold a 450 W solar array. These are quite subtle, so for most people, this van could pass as a standard van and not a camper.
Inside is where you'll find the biggest transformation. Instead of an empty cargo van interior, you'll be greeted by a bright, well-organized interior. It has a closed layout, with the driver's cabin mostly separated from the living space.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / LiamTheTerrible I said "mostly separated" because there's no wall like you'd find in most vans with closed layouts. Instead, the kitchen is the dividing part, but it leaves a bit of space to let some light shine through.
You could even jump from one area to the other if needed in an emergency. What's more, if you want privacy or to block the light coming from the cabin, you can use a roll-down curtain to separate the two areas. Above it, there's a spacious headliner shelf offering storage space.
Regarding aesthetics, the customer opted for wood-imitating vinyl plank flooring, white laminated cabinetry, and a white clad ceiling. The look is complemented by a butcher block countertop, teal couch cushion upholstery, and a blue tiled backsplash.
The kitchen features a black fridge with a tiny freezer compartment, a single-burner induction stovetop with a hinged top, and a pop-up socket that offers standard plugs and USB outlets. What's more, a Maxxair vent fan above is perfectly positioned to draw out the smells and fumes from cooking.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / LiamTheTerrible An overhead shelf with a bungee cord, a drawer, a cabinet underneath the stove, and a cupboard are available for storage. What's more, there are two units by the entrance, each with a top and three shelves – the best part about them is that they're curved so you don't hurt yourself if you bump into them.
Next, we have a floor-to-ceiling unit on the passenger side. It has a closet with a hanging rail, as well as a cupboard with three shelves.
The rear part of the living space seems relatively simple at first sight. It comprises two long benches with backrests, one on each side, and a Lagun table mount with a decently sized top.
Four or more people can sit comfortably here and enjoy a meal or play some board games. You'll also notice five overhead cabinets, a massive wall niche with two bungee cords, and a compartment closer to the kitchen that houses a portable toilet.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / LiamTheTerrible There's more than meets the eye in this part of the van. First, the benches have hinged tops that can be lifted to reveal storage spaces. This is usually where you also find the utility systems – but not in this van.
Since there's no sink or shower in the rig, there's no plumbing system. As for power, Coalition Vans managed to fit the electrical system in the driver's cabin, below the passenger bench and behind the driver's seat. Its highlights are a 460 Ah battery bank and a 2,000 W inverter.
Three charging sources are available: solar power , shore power, and DC-DC charging while the engine is running. If used correctly and efficiently, you could technically never run out of power, especially since the van has just two big power consumers: the fridge and the stove.
The panel behind the driver-side bench is actually not a wall. Pull it down by using a small cut-out, and you'll discover that it's part of a Murphy bed system. The panel folds all the way down, revealing a mattress, charging points, and a wall niche that mirrors the one on the opposite side.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / LiamTheTerrible All in all, this fresh conversion by Coalition Vans keeps things simpler but still manages to pack a surprising amount of comforts inside a compact interior.
What makes this project even more impressive than what we've already seen is that the whole interior was hand-built. Even though each van they make is different, Coalition Vans takes time to create each design by hand, not by using CNC machines like most converters.
